result.question: Explain the mechanism of the onset of the south-west monsoon in India. How do its two branches shape the spatial pattern of rainfall across the country? (Answer in 250 words)

directives.meaning: Make clear how and why it happens: causes, the steps in between, and the effects.

sentences.text: The south-west monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings the bulk of India's annual rainfall.
Its onset results from the interplay of surface pressure, the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and upper-air jet streams.
Intense heating of the north-western plains in May deepens a thermal low over the subcontinent.
The ITCZ shifts northwards and in July lies over the Gangetic plain as the monsoon trough.
Attracted by this low, the south-east trades cross the equator and, deflected by the Coriolis force, blow from the south-west.
In the upper air, it is the westerly jet stream, positioned over the peninsula, that is held responsible for the sudden burst of the monsoon.
The monsoon normally reaches the Kerala coast in early June and then advances rapidly northwards.
The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats, giving heavy orographic rain on the windward slopes, while the Deccan interior lies in a rain-shadow.
Another arm moves along the Narmada and Tapi valleys into central India, while a third crosses Kachchh, giving only scanty rain to western Rajasthan.
The Bay of Bengal branch is deflected towards India by the Arakan Hills and splits into a westward flow along the Ganga plains and a northward flow up the Brahmaputra valley.
A sub-branch strikes the Meghalaya plateau, where Mawsynram, on the crest of the Garo hills, receives the world's highest average annual rainfall.
The Tamil Nadu coast stays relatively dry, lying parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch and in the rain-shadow of the Arabian Sea branch.
Closer monitoring of the jet streams and of ocean-atmosphere links such as ENSO is therefore vital for reliable monsoon forecasts and farm planning.
